High-dimensional data and computational aspects

Gianluca Sottile

Source: vignettes/islasso-highdim.Rmd
islasso-highdim.Rmd

The induced smoothed lasso works with full p \times p matrices (the derivative of the smoothed estimating equation and the sandwich covariance matrix), so its cost grows with the number of covariates. This vignette summarises how islasso keeps the computations manageable.

Cost per iteration

step until 1.6.2 from 1.7.0, p \le 2n from 1.7.0, p > 2n
estimating equation at fixed s.e. damped fixed point, one p\times p Cholesky per step undamped MM (or Newton) steps, one Cholesky per step n \times n factorisations (Woodbury), O(n^2p)
standard errors full sandwich, \approx 4.3\,p^3 flops diagonal only, \approx p^3 flops diagonal only, O(n^2p)
X^\top W X (Gaussian path) recomputed at every \lambda computed once not needed
Gaussian iterations Fortran entirely in C entirely in C
full covariance matrix every iteration once, at convergence once, O(np^2)

The number of steps needed to solve the estimating equation is also smaller, because the majorise–minimise iterations are not damped any more (inner = "mm", default) or use Newton’s method (inner = "newton").

An example with p \gg n 

library(islasso)
n <- 60; p <- 600
beta <- c(2, -2, 1.5, -1.5, 1, rep(0, p - 5))
sim <- simulXy(n = n, p = p, beta = beta, seed = 1, rho = 0.3)
system.time(fit <- islasso(y ~ ., data = sim$data, lambda = 10))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   6.595   0.080   2.378
fit$internal$mode   # 1 = Woodbury back end
#> [1] 1
summary(fit, pval = 0.01)
#> 
#> Call:
#> islasso(formula = y ~ ., lambda = 10, data = sim$data)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
#> -1.33508 -0.44950  0.03032  0.35238  1.51862 
#> 
#>             Estimate Std. Error     Df z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)   0.1169     0.1122  1.000   1.042  0.29742    
#> X1            1.5168     0.1409  1.000  10.768  < 2e-16 ***
#> X2           -0.6826     0.1633  1.000  -4.179 2.93e-05 ***
#> X3            0.4499     0.1565  0.976   2.874  0.00405 ** 
#> X4           -0.7858     0.1540  1.000  -5.102 3.36e-07 ***
#> X5            0.5313     0.1359  0.999   3.911 9.21e-05 ***
#> X116         -0.3691     0.1301  0.982  -2.838  0.00454 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#>

The same model with the dense back end (one 601 \times 601 factorisation per step):

system.time(fit.d <- islasso(y ~ ., data = sim$data, lambda = 10,
                             control = is.control(solver = "dense")))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  35.404   0.198   9.024
max(abs(coef(fit) - coef(fit.d)))
#> [1] 2.706863e-13

Practical advice

  • Use islasso.path() to explore the tuning parameter: with the Gaussian family X^\top W X is computed once, and the models for the different values of lambda are independent, so they can be fitted in parallel with control = is.control(ncores = 4).
  • control = is.control(inner = "newton") usually needs fewer factorisations when p is large.
  • An optimised BLAS/LAPACK library (OpenBLAS, Apple Accelerate, Intel MKL) speeds up all the computations, since the numerical core relies on BLAS level 3 and LAPACK routines.
  • The full covariance matrix is p \times p: with tens of thousands of covariates its storage (8 bytes per entry) becomes the limiting factor.
